title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Valencia’s Streets!
description: Watch how Bidirectional Dijkstra finds the fastest path by growing two shortest-path frontiers—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. This makes the visualization feel dramatically faster while still guaranteeing optimal routes.
ig_caption:
🚦 Valencia (Ruzafa) street graph in motion! In this visualization, **Bidirectional Dijkstra** runs two synchronized searches: one forward from the source and one backward from the destination (on a weighted road network). 🌍

⚙️ **Deep algorithm mechanics:** Dijkstra expands nodes using a min-priority queue based on accumulated cost. Bidirectional Dijkstra maintains *two* priority queues and “meeting” logic—when the forward and backward explored regions overlap, you can compute the best candidate path and stop early once no shorter path can exist. ✅ This reduces explored area compared to single-direction search, while preserving **optimality on non-negative edge weights**.

📌 **Graph theory on real maps:** Each intersection is a node, each road segment is an edge with weight (e.g., distance or travel cost). The algorithm effectively solves a shortest path problem on a weighted graph derived from real street geometry—turning city streets into mathematics you can watch.

👉 Want more pathfinding with real-world maps? Like, follow, and drop a comment: **start/end landmarks** in your city for the next run! 🔁
fb_caption:
🚗💡 Ever wondered how computers find the fastest route on real streets? This reel visualizes **Bidirectional Dijkstra**, a graph-search method that expands shortest-path trees from both the start and the goal until they meet—often exploring fewer nodes than one-way Dijkstra while still guaranteeing the shortest path on non-negative weights.

🧠 Think of intersections as nodes and road segments as weighted edges. Want to see this algorithm on a different neighborhood next? Share this post and comment your chosen start + destination points!
